newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania's ethnic Hungarians united against Iliescu.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania's ethnic Hungarians united against Iliescu.

text.p: Romania's ethnic Hungarians are furious at President Ion Iliescu over what they see as his attempts to pit them against majority Romanians. They want him out of office in this week's election.
To a man, villagers in the patchwork forest areas of Transylvania, where most of Romania's 1.6 million Hungarians live, will vote on Sunday for his rival, Emil Constantinescu.
"We'll all vote for Constantinescu. Iliescu won't get a single vote," said Sandor Gall, local leader of the Hungarian Democratic Union (UDMR) representing minority interests.
"Iliescu has made a big mistake by calling us separatists and traitors. This is nonsense. Why does he want to sow discord between us and Romanians?."
Romanians and Hungarians have had an uneasy relationship for centuries in central Europe. Courting ethnic Hungarian votes, has become an important factor in Sunday's second round vote.

Iliescu, a Moscow-trained communist, beat Constantinescu by four points in the first round. But the opposition Democratic Convention (CDR) won simultaneous parliamentary polls and is about to throw Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy out of government.
Constantinescu's chances in the presidential run-off were boosted when the third-placed candidate, former prime minister Petre Roman asked supporters to back him.
In fourth place with six percent was the UDMR's Gyorgy Frunda, solidly backed by disciplined Hungarian voters.
After the first round, Iliescu accused the UDMR leadership of plotting Yugoslav-style secession from Romania.

"There are UDMR leaders who say that only autonomy and federalisation of Romania could ensure the interests of the Hungarian minority," Iliescu told supporters in the Transylvanian town of Alba Iulia.

His vitriol was surprising a mere two months after he signed an historic treaty with Hungary burying for good any suggestion that Budapest might one day recover Transylvania, once ruled by the Austro-Hungarian empire.
Romanians have bitter memories of Hungarian rule. Austro-Hungary subjected them to discrimination and Hungarian fascists committed atrocities in World War Two.
The pact, seen in Romania as vital to its ambition to move closer to Europe and NATO, also guaranteed minority rights.
"Absolutely ridiculous," the independent daily Adevarul said of Iliescu's speech. "In the pure Stalinist mould."
The 6,500 residents of Corund, 300 km (180 miles) northwest of Bucharest, were confident most Romanians would reject allegations that Hungarians posed a threat to national unity.

"I'm confident Romanians will realise these are nothing but communist lies," Ravasz Domokos, a carpenter, said as he chopped wood by his home. "We are not Romania's enemies. All we want is our rights, to live peacefully with everybody."

Ethnic Hungarians demand more autonomy, including language rights in universities and courts. They also want a larger part of regional budgets, currently determined by central government, to be turned over to local budgets.
"Iliescu is desperate for votes," UDMR leader Frunda told Reuters. "He is playing a dangerous nationalist card without thinking about the consequences."

The bespectacled Frunda, a lawyer from the heart of Transylvania, says his score in the opening round showed he was right to launch a crusade last month "to knock down the Berlin Wall" of distrust between Romanians and Hungarians.
"I wanted to revive the old Transylvanian spirit making it possible for Romanians, Hungarians and Germans to live together," he said. "And I won. Even Romanians voted for me."
But including the UDMR in a future government would be fraught with political risks for Constantinescu's CDR.
Iliescu seized on the issue, saying putting ethnic Hungarians into office would create a "worrying situation". He vowed to defend Romania's unity "with all my energy".

Unlike most villages nestled in hills dotted with fir and oak woods, Corund -- Korond in Hungarian -- bustles with shops displaying colourful local pottery. This draws tourists and supplements incomes. Newly-built houses are common.
Things are far worse in nearby Aita. There are no telephones. Rains turn narrow clay streets into rivers of mud.
But there will be no votes for Iliescu here either.
"We are fed up with Iliescu's promises. Nothing has changed here since 1989," Aita resident Edith Nagy said. "Let's hope life will be better with Constantinescu as president."
